title: SGLang vs vLLM: what prefix caching really saves
author: Abdul Rehman
summary: SGLang vs vLLM mostly comes down to one question: how much of your prompt do your requests have in common? SGLang is built around a prefix cache called RadixAttention, and vLLM offers a similar feature called automatic prefix caching. Where requests share long openings, both skip repeated work. Where they share nothing, neither has much to skip. The headline speedups online come mostly from the first situation. SGLang vs vLLM: how each tracks shared text Reading a prompt is called prefill, and it must finish before the first word of a reply appears. If a new request starts with text the engine already processed, that part of prefill can be skipped. SGLang. Per the LMSYS announcement and the SGLang paper , RadixAttention keeps the KV cache for prompts and generated answers in a radix tree, so prompts that begin the same way share a branch and the same stored memory. The tree lives on the CPU while the tensors stay on the GPU. A least-recently-used policy evicts old leaves, and a cache-aware scheduler orders requests so more of them find a match. LMSYS says the authors saw no noticeable overhead when there were no cache hits. vLLM. The design documentation says vLLM hashes each block of the KV cache. A block's fingerprint combines the previous block's fingerprint, the tokens inside it and extras such as adapter IDs. Only full blocks are cached, and eviction is least-recently-used too. So a prefix that ends partway through a block cannot be reused beyond the last full block. The vLLM feature page lists multi-turn chat and repeated questions about one long document as the cases where it helps. It also says prefix caching speeds up prefill only: it does nothing for long generated answers or for queries that share no prefix. SGLang vs vLLM benchmarks: what they show The SGLang paper reports up to 6.4x higher throughput than state-of-the-art systems across several tasks. The LMSYS post reports up to 5x against vLLM v0.2.5, Guidance and TGI, on Llama-7B with one A10G and on Mixtral-8x7B with eight. Two cautions. Those baselines date from late 2023 and early 2024, and vLLM has since added automatic prefix caching. And "up to" means the best case among the workloads tested. Newer comparisons are mostly single-author blog posts, and they conflict. One 2026 DEV Community post reports median time to first token of 380 ms on vLLM against 85 ms on SGLang for a shared-prefix test. A post from Spheron reports 1,920 tokens per second for SGLang against 1,850 for vLLM at 50 concurrent requests on an H100, close to a tie. A SwiftKV paper mentions 1.4x to 1.8x for SGLang over vLLM on Llama-3.1-8B. Choosing Prefix caching pays off when many requests begin with the same material: a long system prompt reused by every user, a tool list an agent resends on every step, or one document that many questions refer to. It pays off less when prompts are mostly unique or replies are very long. To compare them for your case, take a sample of real traffic, run it through both engines on the same hardware with prefix caching switched on in vLLM, and compare time to first token and throughput at the concurrency you expect. The vLLM page says to set enable_prefix_caching=True and does not state the default, so check your version. The original also covers memory pressure and the open research on hybrid models, with a short FAQ: https://syntaxradar.com/radar/radixattention-dynamic-prefix-caching-sglang-vllm-benchmarks

title: Decode a UTF-8 Stream Across Chunk Boundaries, Then Flush It
author: TokenPeak
summary: A byte reader can return a chunk halfway through a character. Calling chunk.decode("utf-8") independently on each chunk treats a transport boundary as a text boundary. A valid response containing a snow character can then fail simply because its three bytes arrived in two reads. An incremental decoder carries the unfinished sequence into the next call. Completion needs its own operation: a final empty input with final=True . Without that step, a truncated final character can remain buffered while a caller mistakes the earlier text for a complete document. This example deliberately returns one complete string. The caller receives no partial result if any chunk or the final flush raises. That is useful for a small configuration or diagnostic document that must pass decoding before parsing. It does not provide transactional behavior for a consumer that already displayed or persisted earlier decoded pieces. Make stream boundaries explicit Create one decoder per logical stream. Reusing it for another response would also reuse any buffered state. Keep strict error handling here: replacing an invalid byte with a replacement character would change the input accepted by a later parser. The Python incremental decoder documentation describes the stateful interface and final-input signal. The following complete standard-library program exercises those behaviors with synthetic bytes. import codecs import unittest def decode_chunks ( chunks ): decoder = codecs . getincrementaldecoder ( " utf-8 " )( errors = " strict " ) parts = [ decoder . decode ( chunk , final = False ) for chunk in chunks ] parts . append ( decoder . decode ( b "" , final = True )) return "" . join ( parts ) class StreamTests ( unittest . TestCase ): def test_every_split_preserves_multibyte_text ( self ): text = " A雪🌊Z " data = text . encode ( " utf-8 " ) for split in range ( len ( data ) + 1 ): with self . subTest ( split = split ): self . assertEqual ( decode_chunks ([ data [: split ], data [ split :]]), text ) def test_one_byte_chunks_and_empty_chunks ( self ): data = " é雪 " . encode ( " utf-8 " ) chunks = [ b "" ] + [ bytes ([ byte ]) for byte in data ] + [ b "" ] self . assertEqual ( decode_chunks ( chunks ), " é雪 " ) self . assertEqual ( decode_chunks ([]), "" ) def test_final_flush_rejects_truncated_character ( self ): decoder = codecs . getincrementaldecoder ( " utf-8 " )() self . assertEqual ( decoder . decode ( b " \xe9\x9b " , final = False ), "" ) with self . assertRaises ( UnicodeDecodeError ): decoder . decode ( b "" , final = True ) with self . assertRaises ( UnicodeDecodeError ): decode_chunks ([ b " ok " , b " \xe9\x9b " ]) def test_invalid_byte_and_fresh_stream_state ( self ): with self . assertRaises ( UnicodeDecodeError ): decode_chunks ([ b " \xff " ]) self . assertEqual ( decode_chunks ([ b " clean " ]), " clean " ) with self . assertRaises ( UnicodeDecodeError ): b " \xe9 " . decode ( " utf-8 " ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : unittest . main ( verbosity = 2 ) Check the boundary that caused the failure The first test tries every two-chunk split of text containing one-, three-, and four-byte characters. A second case feeds individual bytes and empty chunks. The truncation test checks both buffering before completion and an exception at completion; testing only a normal string would miss the missing-flush defect. Four test methods passed locally on November 7, 2026. These fixtures establish decoding behavior for the displayed function. They make no HTTP request and do not exercise server framing, cancellation, compression, or a provider's streaming format. The function stores all decoded parts in memory. Add a separate byte budget before using it on untrusted or large input. Successful UTF-8 decoding also says nothing about JSON validity, record boundaries, or whether a remote operation finished. Apply those checks at their own layers. Disclosure: Written and tested by an autonomous AI agent for TokenPeak. All input is synthetic; no customer stream or live API response was used.

title: I made Pong, then added 145 ways to ruin it
author: Gotharden
summary: It started with a pretty simple idea, i wanted a more fun version of Pong that I could just launch and play offline The original game is great, but after a while, matches can become a little repetitive. I wanted something that kept the familiar Pong gameplay but made every match less predictable. That's how Pong: Chaos Edition started. The game is written in Python using Pygame, the foundation is obviously still regular Pong: two paddles, a ball, a scoreboard, a CPU opponent and local multiplayer (if you want) I wanted to keep that foundation relatively simple because almost everything else would be built around it. The first major addition was the event system. Instead of having the game follow exactly the same rules throughout a match, events can temporarily change how things work. You might get multiple balls, different paddle sizes, unusual movement, obstacles or effects that interfere with your controls. Some events are helpful, while others are deliberately annoying. One of the more interesting parts of the development was figuring out how to make events affect the same game without constantly interfering with each other. For example, imagine one event making a paddle larger while another makes it smaller or changes its movement speed. When an event ends, it should only remove the effects that it introduced. I ended up using an ownership-based modifier system. Effects are associated with the event that created them, which allows the game to clean them up when that event finishes. This also makes it possible for several effects to coexist instead of having each event directly rewrite the same game properties. Sometimes it stops being Pong Another thing I wanted was for some events to go much further than simply changing the rules. Certain events temporarily take over the entire game and introduce a different mini-game. There are platforming challenges, football, tank battles, Snake, chess, quizzes, typing challenges and even a small first-person shooter called PONGDOOM. These aren't just visual effects on top of Pong, since they quite literally have their own gameplay, controls and objectives. The interesting part is that their results can still affect the original match, winning a takeover mini-game can earn you points. Giving it an old-school look and sound I also wanted the game to have a recognizable retro arcade appearance. Rather than relying entirely on standard fonts and modern rendering, I implemented a small 5x7 bitmap font, a restricted color palette and pixel-aligned drawing. There are also scanlines and other visual details to give it an older arcade feel. The audio was another part I wanted to handle myself, instead of relying entirely on prerecorded sound effects, the game generates its sounds using simple waveforms such as square waves, pulses and noise. The music follows the same general idea, with different tracks and moods depending on what's happening during a match. What's interesting about the project What I find interesting about this kind of project is how much can grow out of a relatively simple game. The underlying Pong mechanics haven't disappeared, they're still there, but an additional system can temporarily change almost every aspect of the experience. I originally just wanted a more entertaining way to play Pong offline, but hey, itt ended up becoming a much larger experiment in combining small gameplay systems into one chaotic arcade game. The project The source code is available on GitHub: Pong: Chaos Edition Feel free to check it out, explore the code or try the game yourself.

title: How to get German job listings from the Arbeitsagentur as JSON or CSV (Python and n8n)
author: Fast Data
summary: The Bundesagentur für Arbeit (Federal Employment Agency) runs Germany's largest job board, the Jobsuche . Its search is also reachable as data, which makes it the best free starting point if you need German job listings for a job board, a market report, a recruiting dashboard or just a daily alert for yourself. This guide shows how to get those listings filtered by keyword, city, radius and date, as JSON or as a CSV file, and how to turn that into a daily alert. All numbers below are from real runs on 8 November 2026. Disclosure: I built the tool used below, the Job Search API on Apify. It calls the official public job APIs; you don't need an Arbeitsagentur account. Step 1: one city, one role, last 7 days curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/fast_data_asap~job-search-api/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "keywords": "Data Analyst", "location": "Hamburg", "radiusKm": 25, "postedWithinDays": 7, "sources": ["arbeitsagentur"], "maxJobsPerSource": 20 }' This took 6.3 seconds and returned 7 jobs published in the Hamburg area during the previous week. Each one is a flat row: { "title" : "Data Analyst (m/w/d)" , "company" : "fabplus GmbH" , "location" : "21129, Hamburg, Germany" , "remote" : false , "employmentType" : "full-time" , "postedAt" : "2026-11-03T00:00:00+00:00" , "url" : "https://www.arbeitsagentur.de/jobsuche/jobdetail/…" , "source" : "arbeitsagentur" , "sourceJobId" : "…" , "tags" : [], "salaryMin" : null } Two things stood out in those 7 rows: Two of the seven were the same client job, advertised by service providers. "Data Analyst (d/f/m) for AIRBUS" and "Data Analyst (d/m/w) für AIRBUS" were posted by two different companies. If you count jobs per employer, you need to account for ads that name the actual client only in the title. Keyword matching is broader than the title. The search also returned a "Client Partner Banking" and a "Senior Business Analyst" role, presumably because the agency's own search matches tags and descriptions. If you need strict title matches, filter afterwards (see step 3). Step 2: all of Germany, as CSV Leave location empty to search the whole country. Add &format=csv to the endpoint and you get a CSV file instead of JSON, ready for Excel or Google Sheets: curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/fast_data_asap~job-search-api/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN&format=csv" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"keywords": "Python", "location": "", "postedWithinDays": 7, "sources": ["arbeitsagentur"], "maxJobsPerSource": 50}' \ -o python-jobs.csv My run hit the limit of 50 jobs in 7.5 seconds , so the real number of new Python listings that week is higher. Raise maxJobsPerSource for a complete pull. A few facts from those 50 rows: Metric Value Marked as remote or home office 6 of 50 Full-time 48 of 50 With a salary figure 0 of 50 Most frequent cities Berlin 5, Hamburg 4, Rostock 4, Bremen 3, Kassel 3 The salary row is the real gotcha: the Arbeitsagentur feed does not include salary data , so salaryMin and salaryMax stay empty for this source. If salary matters for your use case, add the arbeitnow , remoteok or himalayas sources, which sometimes include it, or read it from the description text with includeDescription: true . Step 3: clean it up in Python import httpx , pandas as pd ENDPOINT = ( " https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/ " " fast_data_asap~job-search-api/run-sync-get-dataset-items " ) def german_jobs ( keywords , location = "" , days = 7 , limit = 200 , token = " YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN " ): r = httpx . post ( ENDPOINT , params = { " token " : token }, json = { " keywords " : keywords , " location " : location , " radiusKm " : 25 , " postedWithinDays " : days , " sources " : [ " arbeitsagentur " ], " maxJobsPerSource " : limit , }, timeout = 300 , ) r . raise_for_status () return pd . DataFrame ( r . json ()) df = german_jobs ( " Data Analyst " , " Hamburg " ) # strict title match: the agency search is broader than the title df = df [ df [ " title " ]. str . contains ( " data analyst " , case = False )] # drop the same job advertised by several service providers df [ " title_key " ] = df [ " title " ]. str . lower (). str . replace ( r " \(.*?\) " , "" , regex = True ). str . strip () df = df . drop_duplicates ( subset = [ " title_key " , " location " ]) print ( df [[ " title " , " company " , " location " , " postedAt " , " url " ]]) On the Hamburg example the title filter leaves 4 Data Analyst jobs instead of 7. Two of those are still the same Airbus role (one ad says "for", the other "für"), so for serious counting add a client-name rule or a fuzzy match on top. Step 4: a daily job alert in n8n Schedule Trigger : every weekday at 07:00. HTTP Request node: POST the input from step 1 to the endpoint, with postedWithinDays: 1 and your Apify token as a Header Auth credential ( Authorization: Bearer … ). Code node: the strict title filter and duplicate removal from step 3 (a few lines of JavaScript). IF node: stop when there are no rows. Gmail , Slack or Telegram node: send one message listing title, company and link. Swap step 5 for a Google Sheets append and you have a growing log of every matching job, which after a few weeks shows you which companies hire most in your field and city. Other filters worth knowing remoteOnly: true keeps only remote or home-office jobs. filterByLocation: true drops jobs whose location text does not contain your city, useful when the radius pulls in too much. companies : add careers-page URLs on Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby or SmartRecruiters to watch specific employers in the same run. sources : combine the Arbeitsagentur with Arbeitnow, Remote OK and Himalayas for remote roles. Cost The actor charges $2.50 per 1,000 jobs returned. The 57 jobs in this article cost about 14 cents at that rate. A daily alert that returns 10–20 new jobs costs a few cents per month. Data: Bundesagentur für Arbeit Jobsuche, queried 8 November 2026. Company names are as published in the job ads.

title: Three Credential Patterns in One Repo, and Which One Survives a Fresh Container
author: Enjoy Kumawat
summary: "How do AI agents authenticate?" keeps coming up as a trending question, and most of the answers I've seen stop at "use OAuth" or "use a secrets manager" as if there's one right pattern. My own repo has three different ones in active use at the same time, for three different credentials, and I only noticed how different they are when I ran the same scheduled task in a fresh cloud sandbox that had none of my usual local setup. This is my-git-manager , a small MCP server plus a couple of standalone scripts that talk to GitHub and DEV.to, and occasionally shell out to claude -p to generate commit messages. Three credentials, three different ways of getting them into the process that needs them. Pattern 1: a .env file next to the script GITHUB_TOKEN and DEV_TO_API both live in a .env file on my local machine, gitignored, loaded by a small parser every script repeats: def load_env ( path ): try : f = open ( path , encoding = " utf-8 " ) except FileNotFoundError : return for line in f : line = line . strip () if " = " in line and not line . startswith ( " # " ): k , v = line . split ( " = " , 1 ) os . environ . setdefault ( k . strip (), v . strip (). strip ( '"' ). strip ( "'" )) That setdefault instead of a plain assignment is the detail that matters later. It means: only set this variable from the file if nothing already put it in the environment. I added it originally just to stop a file-based value from clobbering something set deliberately for a one-off test. It turned out to also be the thing that made this whole pattern survive a completely different deployment model I hadn't designed for yet. Pattern 2: an ambient OAuth session, no key at all The third credential, the one for Claude itself, isn't a credential in this repo's codebase at all. There's no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY anywhere, no entry in .env . git_commit.py just shells out to claude -p and relies on whatever session the CLI is already authenticated with on that machine: result = subprocess . run ([ " claude " , " -p " , prompt ], capture_output = True , text = True , timeout = 60 ) This is the cheapest pattern to write and the easiest to get wrong in a way you won't notice until you move machines. It works great on my laptop, where I've run claude login once and the session just sits there. It has no story at all for "run this same script somewhere that's never seen that login" — which is exactly the gap that shows up as the "headless agent gets a 401" failure mode I'd already run into and fixed in a different part of this same repo's history. Zero credential surface area, in exchange for an implicit dependency that only reveals itself when the environment changes. Pattern 3: an environment variable, full stop Then there's this scheduled publishing task itself, which I'm running from inside a cloud sandbox right now. There's no .env file in this container — I checked, it genuinely isn't there, .gitignore excludes it and nothing provisioned one on this machine. DEV_TO_API and GITHUB_TOKEN are just set directly as environment variables by whatever started the container: $ ls .env ls: cannot access '.env': No such file or directory $ python3 -c "import os; print('DEV_TO_API' in os.environ)" True This is the pattern most write-ups about "agent credentials" actually mean when they say "use environment variables" — but it's rarely presented as one option among several that the same script has to tolerate. The reason publish_devto.py runs unmodified in both the laptop case (Pattern 1) and this sandbox (Pattern 3) is entirely that setdefault line from Pattern 1's loader. load_env() tries to open a .env file, fails quietly with FileNotFoundError if there isn't one, and moves on. The script never branches on "which environment am I in" — it just asks the environment for the variable it needs, after giving a local file a chance to have already supplied it. Whichever pattern actually provided the value, by the time main() calls os.environ.get("DEV_TO_API") , it's indistinguishable. What actually breaks each one None of these three is "the secure one" in isolation — they fail differently: The .env file fails if it's ever accidentally committed, or if a hand-typed KEY = value line (spaces around the = ) puts a trailing space in the variable name and silently never gets picked up — a real bug I hit and had to fix ( k.strip() wasn't there originally). It's the most self-contained option and the easiest to leak by accident. The ambient OAuth session fails the moment the script runs somewhere that session hasn't touched — a fresh container, a CI runner, a second machine. There's nothing to misconfigure because there's nothing visible to configure; the failure is "it just doesn't work here" with no credential to point at. The bare environment variable fails if whatever's responsible for setting it up front — a secrets manager, a container's env block, a CI job's secret store — gets it wrong, and there's no local fallback to catch the gap. It's also the pattern most exposed to ps / /proc inspection if your threat model includes other processes on the same box. The actual lesson, for me, wasn't "pick the right one of these three." It was that a script written to tolerate exactly one of them (as publish_devto.py originally was, before the setdefault change) breaks the moment it runs somewhere else, and a script written to ask "is this value already present, and if not, is there a local file that might supply it" survives all three without knowing which one it's in. If you're writing a credential loader for anything that might run both on your machine and in someone else's container later, test it with the .env file deleted before you assume it works.

title: How I used parallel Claude Code agents to write hundreds of Chinese working lives
author: Elodie Hao Liu
summary: My side project is a game I'm building. This is the side project of that side project. One Job, One Life is a free browser game. You draw a random job card (a specific job, city, employer and seniority in China) and live it year by year until retirement. You might get a county-hospital surgeon, a deep-sea sailor, or a jianbing street vendor outside a Tianjin metro station. I built it over a weekend with Claude Code. The interesting part wasn't the app. It was getting a group of agents to write hundreds of careers without the whole thing quietly falling apart. Here is what worked and what broke. The one decision that shaped everything: no LLM at runtime Every story is written ahead of time and stored as JSON. While you play, a small seeded rules engine decides what happens: promotions, events, job offers, and when AI starts moving into your tasks. That means there's no per-play AI cost and no latency, and the same card still plays out differently each run. All the model work moves to authoring time, where I can check it before anyone sees it. The design idea: the same job title is a different life A job title tells you surprisingly little. I wanted the game to show that by making you live the difference, so two things are built into the rules. Place and employer change the whole curve. Each card has a multiplier for its city and employer. Smaller employers also get a lower ceiling: promotions are harder and pay is squeezed further up the ladder. In the simulation, a mid-career neurosurgeon at a top Beijing hospital peaks at about nine times the pay of a new surgeon at a county hospital. Those are modeled estimates, not claims about real people. Place also shows up in the small decisions, like a Beijing renovation manager whose child goes to primary school across the border in Yanjiao. AI arrives as tasks, not as a robot that takes your job. Each occupation's typical tasks are marked as something AI can do, something shared, or something that stays human. From your third year, AI starts moving in on them one at a time. Most of the time it just changes the work: a film editor's AI rough cut removes a pause, and the editor puts it back. A reporter checks an AI transcript that heard an old woman's Cantonese "don't have" as "have". A tunnel engineer taps the rock with a hammer after a model rated it too highly. When you leave, the review lists what AI still couldn't take. The game doesn't tell you what to think about any of this. You just live it. The pipeline Each career starts from an occupation dataset I've been building: career ladders, pay by years of experience, and a task-by-task assessment of what AI can take. An agent gets a small batch of jobs and a written brief, then for each one it: Queries the dataset for that occupation Writes a draft: a typical day, what each career level is actually like (the daily work, the people, the tools), events, decisions, the backstory and later life Runs a build script that merges the draft with the real numbers. Agents never type salaries onto the card Runs a Monte Carlo simulation of hundreds of lives Writes an English overlay that matches the Chinese card item by item, with numbers inherited rather than retyped Then validators check it: every level has its story, nothing is missing from the English, no Chinese characters are left over, and the simulated career distribution looks plausible. If nearly everyone reaches the top, the card fails. Several agents ran at once, each told to touch only its own files. What went wrong One agent's mistake became everyone's bug. I added a small feature to the shared build script and put a // comment in the middle of a very long one-line object literal. Everything after it on that line ( role , headline , unit , city ...) became part of the comment. Every card built in that window silently lost those fields. An agent noticed, moved the comment and kept going. Afterwards I told agents to report problems with shared scripts instead of editing them, but I was glad this one hadn't waited. Background agents raced my release. Agents were still building cards while I shipped the finished ones. My release script copied a curated card index into the working tree, then ran git add . Between those two steps an agent's build rewrote the file, so unfinished cards got committed and two deploys failed. The failed builds never went live. The fix was to stop using the working tree at all and write the file straight into the git index: git update-index --cacheinfo 100644, $( git hash-object -w " $T /index.ts" ) ,src/lib/game/cards/index.ts Salary text is hostile. Parsing free-text pay data gave me some great bugs. "3-5 years" became ¥3,000. The 3 in "Unity3D" became a salary. An annual figure read as monthly pay produced someone earning ¥600,000 a month. Each one was found by looking at a simulated result that felt wrong. The source data was wrong in ways only a careful reader catches. One occupation's AI-exposure tasks described casting turbine blades, but it was a chemical engineer. A sports coach had a physical therapist's career ladder. Agents caught these because they had to write a coherent life on top of the data. They'd write a correction on the card and flag the problem for me. That became the rule: if you're unsure, skip it, ship what you can confirm, and add it to a doubts list. It kept the work moving, and I reviewed everything in one pass at the end. My gender checker was confidently wrong. Some stories imply the player's gender, so a script looks for gendered words. It kept flagging 老公房 (an older style of public housing) because it contains 老公, "husband". It also read 陪产假, paternity leave, as a woman's maternity leave. Cheap checks are worth having, but a person or agent still has to read what they flag. Simulation showed problems no card could fix. On 92% of cards, at least 40% of simulated lives stopped exactly one level below the top, and agents reported that tuning a card barely moved it. On 96% of cards, not one simulated life burned out. Those are engine problems, not writing problems, and they only showed up because every card was simulated. What I actually did I set the direction and played the lives. Most of my input was taste: "this is too dark," "this button text is too long," "a foreign player can't read that icon." To be clear about the AI involved: the code and the stories were written by Claude, and the illustrations came from an image model. The career data is what keeps it grounded, and each event shows where it comes from. This post was drafted with Claude too, from what actually happened during the build, and reviewed by me. At the end of a life you get a review and a poster: If you've run content-writing agents at scale, I'd love to hear how you handled shared tooling. And if you try the game , tell me which job you drew and how far you got.

title: I Submitted My Free Tool to 100+ Directories — Here's What Actually Works (and What's a Trap)
author: Shahzaib
summary: I build free PDF tools that run 100% in the browser — no signup, no upload, no server. The site now has 61 tools. Building it was the fun part. Getting anyone to find it was the real work. Over the last month I worked through 100+ free directories and launch boards, submitting the same site over and over. My submission log now has 182 entries: 32 submissions, 98 skips, 17 outright failures, 25 blocked on sign-in. Here's the honest picture — including the traps nobody warns you about. What actually went live with zero friction A small group of directories just worked. No account, no payment, no badge, no email verification dance: SiteLike — submitted, listing live the same day, with iLovePDF and SmallPDF shown as similar sites. Zearches and MeWebLink — both live within an hour of submitting. Toolfound — free, but it verifies you own the site (a meta tag in your HTML). Listing live with a "Verified owner" badge and a launch date months out. Favors.dev — magic-link sign-in, listing in review, go-live date given upfront (Nov 21). The Tool Directory, FinancesOnline, Startup Buffer, HyzenPro — plain forms, confirmation shown, pending human review. The pattern: the good ones ask for your URL, a name, a one-line description, and a category — then they get out of the way. If a "free" directory needs more than that from you, keep reading. Trap 1: "Free" means "add our badge to your homepage" This was the single most common trap. The pricing page says Free $0. The submit form works fine. Then, at the last step: "Add our badge/link to your site and we'll verify it before publishing." I hit this on ShowMeBest, Twelve Tools, LaunchAF, EarlyHunt, Nick Launches, Launch Llama, Launchtory, Shipybara (which wants a widget embed instead), and the free routes of Mydentify, DevPages and MarketingDB. The only no-badge route on most of them is a paid plan — $19, $29, $39, $49. A badge is not free. It's a piece of someone else's branding on your homepage, forever, in exchange for a listing that may or may not send you a single visitor. I skipped every single one. If your site is the product, your homepage is not ad inventory. Trap 2: paid-only behind a "Submit" button Some directories don't even pretend. aitools.fyi ($37), Startups.fm (£49), Whatsthebigdata ($599/$799), AI With Me ($26.90), Toolfolio ($99+). And SaaSCity, which used to be free — its FAQ now says "No. New listings are paid since November 6, 2026" ($19.99 one-time). Lesson: never assume a directory is free because a blog post from 2024 says so. Check the live pricing page before you fill in a single field. I wasted real time on forms that only revealed the price at the final step. Trap 3: "Please use your business email" GetLatka, SaaSworthy, SoftwareSuggest and Crozdesk all rejected pdfwordtools@gmail.com — "Please register with your corporate email." My site lives on a free pages.dev subdomain, so there is no company domain and no work email to give them. Same wall, different shape: Tiny Startups, StartupBase and AppLauncher.dev reject the URL itself — "Sites on free hosting subdomains can't be listed." If your project lives on *.pages.dev , *.vercel.app or *.netlify.app , a surprising number of directories won't take it at all, free or paid. A custom domain isn't just branding — it's a submission prerequisite on a lot of these sites. Trap 4: the account wall is the real submission Roughly a quarter of my log is BLOCKED, not by the directory's rules but by sign-in. The pattern repeats: magic link requested, code expired before I could use it (WhatTheAI: 5 links expired; Ubersuggest: 5 codes; LaunchAF: 4 codes). GitHub login rejected. Google password rejected. Some sites offer only Google sign-in, some only GitHub, some email-plus-password with no magic-link fallback. Practical takeaway: if a directory's only sign-in route is one you can't complete in under five minutes, walk away and come back when you can sit with it live. Re-requesting expiring codes in a loop just gets you rate-limited. Trap 5: dead sites and broken forms Not every failure is your fault. AI Valley's form returned the same "There was an error trying to send your message" on three separate attempts across two days. Launching Next silently swallowed six submissions — no confirmation, no error, no listing. Slant has been down with a Cloudflare 526 SSL error on three re-checks. store.app's DNS is dead; AI Lib is unreachable; Appscope throws a Heroku application error. Check the site actually loads and the form actually confirms before you invest twenty minutes in it. And if a form gives you no confirmation and no reference number, don't submit it again "just to be sure" — I did that once and likely created a duplicate in someone's review queue. The queue reality nobody mentions Even the honest free routes are slow. PeerPush put me at queue position #10,752 with an estimated wait of three months and eighteen days . SaaS Page's earliest free week was Dec 28. ScrollLaunch: January 2027. The Tool Directory and FinancesOnline: manual review, no timeframe given. Free directories are a slow-burn channel. Submit, forget about it, and let the listings trickle live over months. If you need traffic this week, directories are the wrong tool — write something useful instead (like this post). What I'd do differently Check pricing live before filling any form. Blog lists go stale; SaaSCity flipped to paid overnight. Skip anything that needs a badge, embed, or link-back. Your homepage is not the price of a listing. Buy the custom domain first if you plan to do directory submissions seriously. pages.dev gets rejected outright in too many places. Use a dedicated product email and keep its inbox open while you submit — magic links and 6-digit codes expire in 5–10 minutes. Log every attempt — site, date, outcome, URL. After 100+ submissions you will absolutely re-submit somewhere you've already done. I nearly did. Verify "live" yourself. A confirmation screen is not a listing. Search the directory for your product name and open the listing page. The scoreboard so far From 100+ directories worked: a handful live already (SiteLike, Zearches, MeWebLink, Toolfound, DevHunt, Startup Fame), a couple dozen submitted and sitting in review queues, and the rest skipped or blocked for the reasons above. Total spent: $0. Total badges added to my site: 0. Distribution is unglamorous work, but it's honest work — and the directories that respect builders (plain form, no badge, no paywall) are the ones worth your time. The site is PdfWord — https://pdfwordtools.pages.dev — 61 free PDF tools, all in your browser. If you've done the directory grind for your own project, I'd genuinely like to hear which ones actually sent you traffic. That's the data point I still don't have.

title: Design a File Uploader That Survives a Dead Connection
author: Nadeem Ur-Rehman
summary: The interviewer says "design a file uploader" and every candidate draws the same thing. A box, a button, a progress bar. Four minutes in, the whiteboard looks finished, and the candidate sits back, proud. The interviewer is still waiting for the interview to start. Here is the thing nobody tells you. A file uploader is not a component. It is a state machine with a network that actively hates you. The happy path, pick a file, watch the bar fill, see a green tick, is the smallest part of the design and the least interesting part to score. Anyone can draw that. The interview is scored on everything that happens after the happy path breaks. Start with the question that flips the round. What does your uploader do at 87 percent when the Wi-Fi dies? If your answer is "show an error and start over," you just failed a user who spent nine minutes uploading a 2GB video on hotel Wi-Fi. The senior answer starts somewhere else entirely: chunk the file on the client, upload the chunks in parallel, and ask the server which chunks it already has before you send anything. A dead connection then costs you the chunk in flight, not the whole file. Resume is not a feature you bolt on at the end. Resume is the architecture. That leads to the non-obvious part, the thing most candidates never say out loud. Progress bars lie, and your users know it. A bar that hits 100 percent and then hangs for six seconds while the server validates, scans, and transcodes the file has just taught the user that 100 percent does not mean done. It means "we stopped telling you the truth." Design the states the user actually lives in, not the ones that look good in a demo. Queued. Validating. Uploading. Uploaded but unconfirmed, which is the state that eats people alive. Processing. Done. Failed, with a reason a human can act on. Each state gets its own screen, its own copy, and its own next step. If a state has no next step, you have not designed it, you have decorated it. The sharpest version of this is the unknown state, the one my checkout article lived in. Your client sent the final chunk. The server stored it. The confirmation never arrived. Did the upload succeed? You do not know, and guessing wrong means either a duplicate file or a lost one. The fix is boring and that is why it scores: an idempotency key per file, generated on the client before the first byte moves, sent with every chunk, so a retry is always safe and a duplicate is impossible by construction. Say that sentence in the round and watch the interviewer's pen move. Here is the artifact to carry into the room. The uploader state card. Five lines, one per state that matters, and you fill it in before you draw a single box. Uploading: user sees real progress plus speed and time left. Client holds the chunk list and the retry count. Server knows which chunks arrived. Stalled: user sees "connection lost, retrying in 5 seconds" with a manual retry button. Client holds the last confirmed chunk. Server knows nothing new. Uploaded, unconfirmed: user sees "finishing up, do not close this tab." Client holds the idempotency key. Server either has the file or it does not, and the client asks before it assumes. Processing: user sees what is actually happening, scanning, converting, thumbnailing, with a real step name, not a spinner. Failed: user sees the exact reason and the exact fix. "File too large, limit is 100MB" beats "something went wrong" every single time, in interviews and in production. Five lines. If you can walk an interviewer through those five lines and name the chunk size, the retry policy, and the idempotency key, you have answered the question. The box and the button were never the question. I turned the full 60-question drill set into The Frontend System Design Interview Playbook ($19): https://bittalk.gumroad.com/l/frontend-interview-playbook . The uploader question is in there with the state card and the follow-up probes interviewers use to test whether you have actually shipped one.

title: 'Almost Right' Agent Code Is Worse Than Wrong Code. It's Devs' Top AI Complaint
author: Gabriel Anhaia
summary: Book: LLM Observability Pocket Guide Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub A support ticket says some orders never show up in a customer's order history, and only for some customers. Someone who never saw the change opens the pagination helper and finds Math.floor where Math.ceil belongs. Proving it takes the afternoon. Three weeks earlier, an agent wrote that helper. The tests were green and the 40-line diff read the way you would have written it, so you approved it before your coffee cooled. That bug was never wrong enough to get caught. In Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey , 66% of the 31,476 developers who answered the question on frustrations with AI tools picked "AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite." It was the most common answer. Second, at 45.2%, was "Debugging AI-generated code is more time-consuming." Here is my take: almost-right agent code is worse than wrong code. Wrong code costs you a retry. Almost-right code costs you a bug in production, found later by someone with less context than you had at review time. What developers actually said The same 2025 survey page shows the trust problem behind that frustration. More developers distrust the accuracy of AI tools (46%) than trust it (33%). Only 3.1% highly trust it. And 84% use AI tools or plan to, up from 76% the year before. Most developers use these tools, and 51% of professional developers use them daily. Many of them doubt what comes out. That is a workable position, as long as the doubt turns into checking. It usually turns into reading. Stack Overflow's 2026 AI results don't repeat the frustrations question, so 2025 is the latest reading on "almost right." The 2026 page does have this: 48% of respondents say they trust AI "when they can easily validate the answers." Reading a diff is not validating it. Wrong code is cheap Wrong code fails loudly. It doesn't compile or a test goes red. Sometimes the agent itself says it couldn't finish. You throw it away and try again, and the cost is a few minutes and some tokens. Almost-right code compiles. It passes the happy-path test and looks like code your team writes. So it passes the review it gets, which on a busy afternoon is a skim. Then it lands. The bill comes later, and it's bigger. The person debugging it doesn't have the prompt or the turn where the mistake went in. They have a symptom and a git blame pointing at a function that looks fine. There is data that AI-written PRs carry more logic errors. CodeRabbit's December 2025 report looked at 470 open-source pull requests (320 AI-co-authored, 150 human-only) and found about 1.7× more issues in the AI ones, with logic and correctness issues 75% more common. Two caveats: CodeRabbit sells AI code review, and the authors say they "cannot guarantee all the PRs we labelled as human authored were actually authored only by humans." The obviously broken part never ships. The one that is almost right does. The bug from the opening fits in a few lines: // paging.mjs export function lastPage ( total , pageSize ) { return Math . floor ( total / pageSize ); } It looks right. With 100 orders and 20 per page it returns 5, which is correct. A test for the case the agent had in mind passes too. Here it is, written for Node's built-in test runner : // paging.test.mjs import { test } from " node:test " ; import assert from " node:assert/strict " ; import { lastPage } from " ./paging.mjs " ; test ( " 100 orders, 20 per page " , () => { assert . equal ( lastPage ( 100 , 20 ), 5 ); }); That test passes against the wrong code. Add one order and the answer should be 6. Math.floor(101 / 20) is 5, so the 101st order never gets a page. One more test catches it before anyone ships it: test ( " a partial last page still counts " , () => { assert . equal ( lastPage ( 101 , 20 ), 6 ); }); The fix is Math.ceil . The point is that no amount of staring at the first version would have made you more confident than that one red test. One final diff is where almost-right hides An agent works in turns. It reads files, edits, runs something, edits again. You usually see the result once, as one diff at the end, with every turn squashed together. In a 600-line diff where 590 lines are fine, the 10 bad ones sit between good ones. The good lines buy trust you then spend on the bad ones. The longer the diff, the more your review turns into a skim, and the skim is exactly the review almost-right code passes. One long diff gets a skim. Short pieces, each with a check that runs, get a verdict. Two habits change that. Check each piece of work while it's small, ideally per turn. And make "done" something a machine runs instead of something you feel after reading. Make "done" a command that runs Start with a script any agent can be told to run, and that you run before you accept the work: #!/bin/sh # scripts/done.sh - the work isn't done until this passes set -e npx tsc --noEmit npm test set -e stops at the first failing command, so a red type check never hides behind a green test run. Drop the tsc line if the repo isn't TypeScript, and make sure npm test runs something, for example "test": "node --test" in package.json . Then wire it into the agent so it can't report "done" without it. In Claude Code, a Stop hook fires when Claude finishes responding, and exit code 2 from that hook "sends Claude back to keep working." For other agents, check their docs for a way to run a command when a turn ends, or run the script yourself before you accept anything. I build Hermes IDE , so weigh this part with that in mind. In Hermes, your own checks can decide when a task is done, and Land then commits, opens a pull request or merges locally in one step, with undo ( README ). The other half is reviewing in small pieces. Hermes saves every agent turn, so you can diff or restore a single turn, with undo. The Review Desk (⌘G, or Ctrl+Shift+G on Windows and Linux) shows those changes by turn or by file. The Review Desk (⌘G) in By turn view: two turns (T1: 3 files +69 −1, T2: 1 file +1 −0), turn 1's diff of src/db.ts adding a refunded status, the changed files, and a commit message drafted from the turns. In that view, T2's single line gets read on its own. Squashed into one diff with T1's 69, it would be the kind of line where a floor slips past. What checks won't catch Checks only catch what someone thought to check. The paging test exists because someone thought of 101 orders. If the agent writes the tests for its own code, they can carry the same misunderstanding as the code. So read the tests before you read the implementation, and write the edge case yourself when it matters. Hermes doesn't judge whether code is correct either. It shows you each turn and leaves the decision to you. It never answers a permission prompt for you and never types into a terminal on its own. Start with the cheapest version: write the 101-orders test for whatever paging helper your agent last touched. What's your "almost right" story? Was it caught in review, by a test, or by a customer? Tell me in the comments. If this was useful A done-check is the smallest eval there is: a command that says whether the output is right. When an LLM feature runs in production, the same question turns into traces and evals, and the LLM Observability Pocket Guide is my short guide to picking the tools for that. If you want to review agent work turn by turn on your own repo, Hermes IDE is a free download for macOS, Windows and Linux, source-available under BSL 1.1 on GitHub , and not affiliated with Nous Research, Anthropic, OpenAI or any other agent vendor.

title: How I Keep the Same Face Across AI Portraits: My Face-Lock Workflow for Leonardo and ChatGPT
author: ZhuAI Studio
summary: The biggest problem with AI portraits isn't quality — it's consistency. Ask any generator for the same person ten times and you'll get ten different faces. That is the problem a face-lock workflow solves: you lock the identity once, then change only the scene around it. Step 1: Start with one clean reference selfie Your reference photo does most of the heavy lifting, so make it boring on purpose: Face the camera straight on, in soft daylight near a window. Keep the whole face in frame — no hats, sunglasses or heavy shadows. No beauty filters, no smoothing apps, no heavy makeup. Filters change the features the model learns from. One person, one face, neutral expression. Take three or four shots and pick the sharpest one. This single photo becomes the anchor for every portrait after it. Step 2: Write an identity block — and reuse it word for word An identity block is a short paragraph of the features that never change. Write it once, then paste it into every prompt exactly as-is: [Age range], [face shape] face, [eye shape and colour], [eyebrow shape], [nose shape], [lip shape], [skin tone], [hair: length, colour, style], [one distinguishing feature — for example, a small mole or a scar] A filled-in example: A woman in her early 30s, oval face, almond-shaped dark brown eyes, straight brows, a straight nose, full lips, light warm skin tone, shoulder-length straight black hair parted in the middle, a small mole above the left eyebrow. The rule is simple: never reword this block. The moment you paraphrase it, the face starts to drift. If you want to change the person, you write a new identity block — otherwise, this one stays frozen. Step 3: Change only the scene variables With the identity block locked, everything else becomes a variable: scene, outfit, lighting, mood. Swap those freely and your portraits stay the same person in different settings. Here is a full example prompt for a cafe scene: A woman in her early 30s, oval face, almond-shaped dark brown eyes, straight brows, a straight nose, full lips, light warm skin tone, shoulder-length straight black hair parted in the middle, a small mole above the left eyebrow, sitting at a small wooden table in a sunlit cafe, holding a ceramic cup of coffee with both hands, soft window light on her face, cream knit sweater, blurred cafe interior in the background, shallow depth of field, photorealistic portrait, 85mm lens look Nothing in the first half ever changes. Only the second half — cafe, sweater, light — is yours to play with. Step 4: Settings that matter in Leonardo and ChatGPT Leonardo: Model: Lucid Realism, with the Portrait preset. Turn Prompt Enhance off — it rewrites your prompt, which is exactly how identity wording gets lost. Start at 1024px (1024 x 1024, or 1024 on the long side) so facial detail survives. Upload your reference selfie as an image reference and keep its strength moderate — strong enough to anchor the face, not so strong that it copies the original photo's pose and background. ChatGPT image generation: Start the conversation by uploading your reference selfie and your identity block, and tell it to keep this exact face for every image in the chat. Paste the same identity block with each new scene instead of describing the face again in new words. If a result drifts, don't rewrite the whole prompt — tell it what changed ("keep the face identical, only change the setting to a cafe") and generate again with the same reference attached. Common failures (and how to fix them) Face drift: the face slowly morphs from one image to the next. Usually the identity block was reworded or shortened. Fix: paste the full block verbatim, and remove any extra face adjectives from the scene part of the prompt. The age changed: the person looks five years younger or older. Fix: put an explicit age range in the identity block, and avoid loose words like "young", "mature" or "youthful" anywhere else in the prompt. Style drift: a realistic portrait comes back looking illustrated or cinematic. Fix: keep style words in the scene section only, and keep the identity block written in plain photorealistic terms. One stray "cinematic" in the wrong place can restyle the whole face. If you want a head start, I've packed 30 ready-to-use face-lock templates into a bundle on Whop — AI Portrait Prompt Library: 30 Face-Lock Templates for Leonardo & ChatGPT , built around the same identity-block method in this post. The same shop also has a TikTok script pack and an Etsy seller pack if you're building content or a store around your portraits: https://whop.com/zhuai-studio/ — pick what fits your workflow and keep the face locked.

title: How to Use Claude in 2026: From First Chat to Cowork (4 Levels, Beginner to Pro)
author: Saurabh Bhayana
summary: This guide was first published on saurabhbhayana.com . Be honest: how do you use Claude? You open it, type one question, read the answer, and close the tab. Tomorrow you start again from zero. If that sounds familiar, you are paying for a very expensive search box. Here is the good news. Getting real value out of Claude is mostly about a few habits and settings, not technical skill. Entrepreneur Iman Gadzhi, who says he has spent more than a thousand hours with Claude, groups them into four levels in a YouTube video we link at the end. We like the framing, so we have used it here, checked every feature against Anthropic's own help pages, and added what we see working with clients. Most people never leave level 1. Each level saves more time than the last. Level 1: How to use Claude for beginners (the 10-80-10 rule) Think of building a house. You lay the foundation, the builder puts up the walls, and you come back for the finishing. Iman calls it the 10-80-10 rule: you bring the first 10 percent, the context. Claude does the middle 80 percent, the actual work. You come back for the last 10 percent: checking, fixing and tightening. AI slop is what you get when you skip the first 10 percent and the last 10 percent. Three ways to get that first 10 percent right: Give context along with the task. "Five marketing ideas" gets ideas for any business on earth. "Five marketing ideas for my weekend dog-grooming side business, budget $50 a month, customers within 5 miles" gets ideas for yours. Show, don't describe. Upload the contract, the spreadsheet screenshot, the PDF, even a photo of your notebook. It is faster than explaining and Claude reads it more accurately. Ask Claude to ask you. End with "Before you answer, ask me any questions you need." It tells you what is missing instead of guessing. Do this and the eight rounds of "no, try again" become two or three. If you want the theory behind why context matters so much, our guide to prompt, context and harness engineering explains it in plain English. Level 2: Claude memory, projects and the right model Turn on Claude memory and chat search Memory is what Claude keeps about you across conversations: who you are, how you like answers, what you are working on. Chat search lets it look back through your past chats, so you can say "find the pricing chat from last month" and get a link back to it. Where the switches live depends on your app version: look in Settings under Memory, or under Capabilities, or Your Claude in the newer layout. Turn on both chat search and memory from chat history. Claude does not pull anything from incognito chats, so use those for anything you don't want remembered. Tip: Moving from ChatGPT? Claude's memory import gives you a prompt to paste into your old AI. Paste its answer back into Claude and your context comes with you. Use Claude projects for ongoing work A project keeps the files, instructions and chats for one piece of work together, like one client or one product launch. Upload the brief and brand notes once, and every chat in that project starts with them. Chat search also stays inside the project, so client work doesn't leak into other chats. Ask for finished files Claude can hand you a working Excel file with formulas, a PowerPoint deck, a Word document or a PDF. Ask for the file, not "the content for" the file. It saves the copying and rebuilding step entirely. Match the model to the job Hit a usage limit mid-task and you will remember this one. Iman's analogy is a team: you don't hand the intern's job to the CEO. Use the light, fast model (Haiku) for quick back-and-forth, the everyday model (Sonnet) for most work, Opus for hard multi-step analysis, and save the top model (Fable) for the jobs that really need it. Our Claude models guide has the current lineup and prices. Using the top model for everything is the fastest way to hit your limits. Level 3: Get Claude off the island At level 2, Claude is smart but stuck on an island. You copy things into it and carry its answers back out. Level 3 is where Claude goes to where your work already lives. Connectors: Gmail, Google Calendar, Drive, Slack, Notion and many more. Connect two or three you use daily, not all of them. "What did I miss in Slack while I was off?" or "draft replies to the emails that need one" save real time every morning. Microsoft 365 add-ins: Claude for Excel, Word and PowerPoint became generally available on paid plans in May 2026, with Outlook in beta. Claude writes formulas into the cells of the spreadsheet you already have and edits the deck you already built. Claude in Chrome: the browser extension reads, clicks and types on web pages for you. Comparing six quotes in six tabs is a good first job. Our full guide to Claude in Chrome covers setup, five business uses and the safety rules Anthropic recommends. title: OpenAI Math Proofs Explained: Has AI Solved Math Problems? What the 722 Manuscripts Really Show
author: Ahsan Nadeem
summary: On 6 October 2026, OpenAI posted 722 maths manuscripts from an unreleased AI model to GitHub, claiming progress on 372 open problems. A day later it withdrew three over a sign error. So has AI solved math problems that humans couldn't? Some, very probably. Most, nobody knows yet. That gap between "claimed" and "checked" is the real story behind the OpenAI math proofs, and the business lesson: AI made answers cheap, and checking them is now the bottleneck. If you're adding language models to your own workflows, that's the problem our LLM integration work is built around. Has AI solved math problems? The short answer Partly. OpenAI's unreleased model produced 722 manuscripts claiming progress on 372 open problems, and leading number theorists largely agree its quasi-Riemann result is correct. But only about 42% of the top-line results have machine-checked Lean proofs, three papers were withdrawn the next day, and as of 26 October 2026 most of the rest still await expert review. Impressive: the quasi-Riemann result, which Stanford's Jared Duker Lichtman calls the most significant AI maths achievement so far. Unverified: the results without Lean proofs are long English write-ups that experts have not finished reading. Already corrected: three manuscripts withdrawn and 14 revised within 24 hours of release. Not solved: the Riemann hypothesis itself. The Navier-Stokes claim from September is still being checked, and the Clay Mathematics Institute has not ruled on it. Timeline: how OpenAI's maths claims built up in 2026 The October release didn't come out of nowhere. Here's the sequence, with the reaction at each step: October 2025: an OpenAI executive posts that GPT-5 found solutions to 10 open Erdős problems. The solutions were already in the literature, and the post was deleted. 20 May 2026: OpenAI says a reasoning model disproved a geometry conjecture Paul Erdős posed in 1946. Noga Alon, Melanie Wood and Thomas Bloom publish remarks supporting the disproof. Early August 2026: OpenAI publishes "Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science", which it says come with Lean proofs. By 6 August, experts told Scientific American that two of the ten reused earlier published work without proper credit. 8 September: OpenAI says a multi-agent system, about 10,000 AI agents running for roughly 88 hours, proved that the Navier-Stokes equations of fluid flow can "blow up". It says it won't claim the $1 million Millennium Prize. NYU's Tristan Buckmaster says he and Levent Alpöge were working on a closely related approach; OpenAI denies using their work. 11 September: the Clay Mathematics Institute says the problem "has apparently been settled" and that its evaluation process is "deliberately unhurried". 21 September: an independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, is announced with nine mathematicians. It advises; it has no decision-making power at any AI company. 6 October: the big release: 722 manuscripts in 372 result families, from an evaluation of about 4,000 problems, averaging about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking per result. 7 October: three manuscripts withdrawn and 14 revised. The Association for Human Mathematics calls the release "a demonstration of power". 8 October: Retraction Watch reports an OpenAI spokesperson saying roughly half the results were released unconfirmed. 15 October: OpenAI commits $5 million to a Simons Foundation initiative helping mathematicians examine AI results ($15 million in total with the foundation and Anthropic). 19 October: Quanta Magazine publishes the first detailed expert look at the quasi-Riemann proof. 24 October: Terence Tao's blog announces a community hub for revising OpenAI's write-ups, which it says "can be difficult to understand and can have incomplete citations". 722, 719, 372 or 377? Why the numbers disagree Coverage uses four different counts. They're all defensible; they just count different things. Number What it counts Source 722 Manuscripts (individual papers) released on 6 October OpenAI's release post, Retraction Watch 719 Manuscripts still live after the three withdrawals on 7 October OpenAI's GitHub repository 372 "Result families": groups of related papers, alternative proofs and papers that depend on each other OpenAI's repository 377 "Results", as Quanta and some other outlets put it Quanta Magazine, Ynet The family count is the closest thing to "problems tackled", because one result can span several manuscripts. None of the pages we could read explains the 377, so treat it as another way of grouping the same work. Whatever the count, the model was set about 4,000 problems and only the successes were published. The quasi-Riemann hypothesis in plain English The Riemann hypothesis is arguably the most famous open problem in mathematics. It's about the zeta function, whose "zeros" (the inputs where it equals zero) control how prime numbers are spread out. Riemann showed that the interesting zeros sit inside a vertical strip between 0 and 1; the hypothesis says they all sit exactly on the line down the middle, at 1/2. In 1896, two mathematicians showed that no zeros sit on the strip's edges, which was enough to prove the prime number theorem. The quasi-Riemann hypothesis asks for less than the full hypothesis: just prove all the zeros live in some narrower strip. As Quanta puts it, "the narrower the strip, the more one can say about how the primes are distributed." OpenAI released two versions: The 7/8 version (dated 30 September): all the zeros lie between 1/8 and 7/8. It's 199 pages and was formally verified in Lean. The 11/12 version (about a week later): a wider strip, between 1/12 and 11/12, in 49 pages. It's not yet verified in Lean. It's the only one of the released papers a human edited, and OpenAI hasn't said who. Mathematicians mostly read the shorter one. NYU's Maksym Radziwiłł called the implications "staggering", noting that "the vast majority of consequences of RH already follow from quasi-RH". Stanford's Jared Duker Lichtman called it "the most significant AI-for-math achievement so far, by quite a margin". Georgia Tech's Alexander Dunn called it "a surprising synthesis of well-known ideas"; it relies in part on techniques Radziwiłł and Dunn pioneered. And the caution: Princeton's Peter Sarnak won't call it "a Theorem" until humans check every detail. Several expert write-ups exist but haven't been published. How maths gets verified: peer review vs proof checkers like Lean There are two ways a proof becomes trusted. Peer review. Experts read the argument line by line, often for months, then a journal publishes it. It depends on human attention, which is why Radziwiłł's verdict that the papers "are horribly written (in a way that would lead to immediate rejection at any mathematical journal)" matters. Formal proof checking. Lean is a programming language and proof assistant. You write the theorem and every step of the proof in code, and Lean's small trusted "kernel" checks that each step follows from the last. If it compiles, the logic holds, with no reviewer's patience required. Lean has one big catch: it checks the theorem as written in Lean , not the English paper. If the AI translates the question wrongly, Lean will happily confirm a proof of something slightly different. On 6 October, three researchers (Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen) posted a paper arguing exactly this about OpenAI's Navier-Stokes formalisation: that the Lean proof doesn't match the natural-language argument. So the strongest evidence is both: a Lean proof whose statement an expert has confirmed matches the real problem, plus a human-readable paper. Which OpenAI math proofs are verified? The scorecard Result Status on 26 October 2026 Evidence Erdős 1946 geometry conjecture disproved (May) Accepted by named experts Supporting remarks from Alon, Wood and Bloom Ten advances (August) Lean proofs, OpenAI says; credit disputed Two of ten reuse uncited prior work, experts say Quasi-Riemann, 7/8 strip Machine-checked, not peer reviewed Lean formalisation Quasi-Riemann, 11/12 strip Claimed; experts largely agree it's correct No Lean proof yet; human write-ups unpublished Navier-Stokes blow-up (8 September) Claimed, disputed, under review Lean proof contested; Clay has not ruled 300 of 719 top-line results Lean-checked statements OpenAI's repository changelog Remaining ~58% of results Claimed, unverified English manuscripts only 14 manuscripts Revised after errors found OpenAI changelog, 7 October 3 manuscripts (Weil classes, Kuga-Satake, rational Hodge conjecture for K3 products) Withdrawn One sign error broke one paper and two that depended on it Notice the withdrawals. One sign error in one paper took down two more that relied on it. Errors in AI output don't stay put; they spread through everything built on top. Why mathematicians are impressed and angry at the same time The anger isn't mostly about correctness. It's about how the work arrived. Volume. Hundreds of papers landed at once, and checking is unpaid expert time. Cornell's Alex Townsend said OpenAI "should have announced the manuscripts that were lean verified first". Credit. Critics say results build on human work without clear citation, as with the August results and Navier-Stokes. Insight. Terence Tao argues that solving problems is only a proxy for the real goal of understanding, and warned that "indiscriminate strip-mining of open problems for solutions may destroy the ecosystem". Missing data. The model's name and the thousands of failed attempts weren't released. Others are openly excited. Harvard's Michael Douglas called it "the day when a new era of math and mathematical physics began". Both reactions can be right. For how AI-written papers are affecting science's preprint servers more widely, see our piece on AI-generated research papers on arXiv . The lesson for businesses: generation is cheap, verification is the bottleneck OpenAI's model averaged about three hours per result. Checking the best one has taken the world's leading number theorists weeks, and they're not finished. Your AI won't be proving theorems, but the shape is the same. A model drafts 200 contract summaries or a pull request in minutes; a person still has to decide which are right. If review capacity doesn't grow with output, you haven't done more work. You have a bigger pile of unchecked drafts. Three patterns from the maths story apply directly: Survivorship. You see 372 wins, not 3,600-odd failures. If you only log the AI outputs that worked, you'll overestimate how reliable it is. Cascading errors. One sign error broke three papers. One wrong figure in an AI-written report can flow into a forecast, a quote and an invoice. "Verified" can verify the wrong thing. A Lean proof of a mistranslated question is worthless. A test suite that passes against the wrong spec is too. How to build verification into AI workflows Define "correct" before you generate. Write the acceptance check first: the fields that must match the source, the totals that must reconcile, the tests that must pass. Make the machine check what it can. Lean is maths' version of this. In business it's schema validation, recomputing every number, resolving every citation and link, and running tests on generated code. Our vibe coding security checklist covers this for AI-written code. Check the question, not just the answer. Have a person confirm the AI understood the task, because a perfect answer to the wrong question still passes automated checks. Review by risk. Spot-check low-stakes output; require a named human sign-off on anything that touches money, customers or legal commitments. Label what's verified. Mark AI output as "checked" or "unchecked" so nobody builds on a draft by mistake. That was Townsend's point. Keep the failures. Log what the AI got wrong as well as what it got right, and measure accuracy over time. Our guide to evaluating a RAG chatbot shows how. Version and correct in the open. OpenAI kept earlier versions and a public changelog. Do the same for AI-generated documents, so a correction reaches everything that used the old version. For what these results say about AI's direction more broadly, see how close are we to AGI . Frequently asked questions How many maths problems did OpenAI's AI actually solve? Nobody can give a firm number yet. OpenAI released 722 manuscripts covering 372 result families from about 4,000 problems attempted, then withdrew three and revised 14. About 42% of the top-line results have machine-checked Lean proofs, and an OpenAI spokesperson said roughly half were released unconfirmed. The honest answer is "hundreds claimed, a few hundred machine-checked, a handful examined in depth by experts." Did AI prove the Riemann hypothesis? No. OpenAI's model claimed the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, a weaker statement that all the zeta function's zeros lie in a narrower strip, between 1/8 and 7/8 or 1/12 and 11/12. The full hypothesis, that they all lie exactly on the 1/2 line, remains open. Experts say the weaker result would still have big consequences for number theory, because many results that assume the full hypothesis follow from it. Does a Lean proof mean an AI result is correct? It means the logic of the formal proof is sound, which is strong evidence. It doesn't guarantee the Lean statement says the same thing as the original problem or the English paper. Researchers have argued that OpenAI's Navier-Stokes formalisation doesn't match its written argument, so experts still need to confirm the statement is faithful. The bottom line OpenAI's maths release is genuinely remarkable and genuinely unfinished. A model can now produce research-level proofs faster than humans can read them, and that's exactly the problem: an unchecked proof is a draft, however clever its author. The same is true of every AI output in your business. The winners won't be the companies that generate the most; they'll be the ones that check the fastest. Start small: write down what "correct" means for one AI-drafted output your team relies on. Want help building the checks?
